title.en: The Iron Chamber and the South Sea at Kandang West
title.zh: 鐵室與西部康丹之南海

region.en: Pakuan Pajajaran and the southern coast (Kandang West)
region.zh: 帕庫安·巴查查蘭與南海岸（西部康丹）

texts.period: Sundanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817), vol. II ch. X

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X (the iron-smith and the king)

summary.en: A youth of the Sundanese court excels in every kind of iron-work, fashioning red-hot iron with his fingers, and is made chief of the smiths. He constructs an iron chamber that attracts the prince, persuades him to step inside, and closes the door — burning him alive, or, in some accounts, casting him into the South Sea at Kandang West, fulfilling the devotee's prophecy. The smith assumes the government, and the Pajajaran succession passes through blood and betrayal — the legend in which the smith's art kills the king and the South Sea receives him.
summary.zh: 巽他宮廷一名青年精於一切鐵藝，徒手拈紅鐵，遂為鐵匠之長。他造鐵室吸引王子，誘其入內閉門——或焚之於室內，或據另說擲之於西部康丹之南海——應了苦行者之預言。鐵匠遂奪政權；帕查查蘭王統由血與背叛傳承——匠人之藝弒王、南海受王之軀。

sensitivity.note: Sundanese dynastic legend; the South Sea at Kandang West is the region later bound to the sea-queen Ratu Kidul.

passages.text: The youth soon excelled in the manufacture of all kinds of iron-work, and in the wild tradition of the country he is said to have fashioned the red hot iron with his fingers; in a short time he was made chief of the Pandi or iron-smiths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having constructed an iron chamber or cage which particularly attracted the attention of the prince, he succeeded in persuading him to step in it; when closing the door, he according to some accounts burned him alive, or according to others caused him to be thrown into the South Sea at Kandang West, thus fulfilling the prophecy of the devotee.

title.en: The Bitter Maja Fruit: How Majapahit Got Its Name
title.zh: 苦摩賈果：馬卓帕希特之名的由來

texts.period: Javanese chronicle tradition (Javan year 1221 / AD 1299), recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the founding of Majapahit

summary.en: Raden Tanduran, defeated and fleeing east with three followers, takes refuge with a widow and with his sister performing penance on Mount Chermai; following the course of a bird she releases for the purpose, he reaches Wirasaba. There he sees the maja fruit entwined round a tree, bites it and finds it extremely bitter, throwing it away — 'Then let us stop here and establish our kingdom, and let us call it Majapahit': the empire named from a mouthful of bitterness.
summary.zh: 敗逃的拉德恩·坦都蘭攜三隨從東行，借宿寡婦之家，又遇其妹在徹瑪伊山修行；他循其妹所放之鳥飛行之路抵維拉薩巴。見纏繞樹上之摩賈果，一口咬下苦不可忍，隨即吐棄——『就停在此建國，就叫它馬卓帕希特（苦摩賈）』——帝國以一口之苦命名。

sensitivity.note: Name-etiology of Majapahit in the chronicle tradition.

passages.text: Raden Tanduran arriving at the river of Grissee took refuge at the house of a widow, and afterwards meeting with his sister, who was performing a penance on the mountain Chermai, he was encouraged by her to proceed further east, following the course of a bird which she desired that he would let loose for the purpose, till he reached the district of Wirasaba.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: Here he observed a plant called the maja, entwined round a tree; he wished to eat of the fruit, but finding it extremely bitter threw it away. 'Then let us stop here and establish our kingdom, and let us call it Majapahit' — for maja and pahit both signify 'bitter' — the name given in the Javan year 1221.

title.en: The Stone Column of Tigil: The Boundary of Two Kingdoms

region.zh: 中爪哇三寶瓏附近提吉勒

texts.period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the treaty of the two princes

summary.en: The armies of Pajajaran and Majapahit meet at the centre of the island, and the general engagement proves indecisive; as the two chiefs are about to close in personal combat, it is mutually agreed that henceforth the countries to the west shall be subject to Pajajaran and those to the east to Majapahit — a line drawn due south from a stone column placed near the spot in commemoration of the agreement. The column is still to be seen at Tigil, a few miles west of Semarang.
summary.zh: 巴查查蘭與馬卓帕希特兩軍會於島之中部，大戰不分勝負；正當兩王將要親自決鬥之際，雙方協定：自此以西諸地屬巴查查蘭、以東屬馬卓帕希特——自主柱石向南畫一直線為界，立柱以紀此約。該柱至今猶存於三寶瓏以西數里之提吉勒。

sensitivity.note: Boundary-treaty legend; the standing column as charter.

passages.text: Both princes moved with their respective armies towards the centre of the island; a general engagement took place, which proving indecisive, a personal combat between the two chiefs was about to occur, when it was mutually agreed that thenceforth the countries to the west should be subject to Pajajaran, and those to the east to Majapahit. A line was drawn due south from a stone column placed near the spot in commemoration of the agreement; the column is still to be seen at Tigil, a few miles west of Semarang.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.

title.en: Brama Hedali and the Eighty Smiths
title.zh: 婆羅摩·赫達利與八十鐵匠

region.en: From Pajajaran to Majapahit across the river Pamali
region.zh: 自帕查查蘭跨帕馬利河至馬卓帕希特

texts.period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the emigration of the smiths

summary.en: Heavy demands made upon the people set off emigrations from Pajajaran: Brama Hedali at the head of eighty Pandi, or iron-smiths, with their families, deserts the country; pursued as far as the river Pamali in Brebes, the smiths effect their escape and are received with open arms at Majapahit. When the king demands that the smiths be delivered up, the refusal is positive — and war follows.
summary.zh: 帕查查蘭苛捐重斂，民乃外遷：婆羅摩·赫達利率八十名鐵匠（Pandi）攜家出走；追兵直逼布利貝斯之帕馬利河，鐵匠們逃脫成功，在馬卓帕希特受到張臂歡迎。王者索要工匠，對方斷然拒絕——戰爭隨之而來。

sensitivity.note: Migration legend; the smith-caste's allegiance as political capital.

passages.text: In a short time considerable emigrations took place from Pajajaran, in consequence of the heavy demands made upon the people: among others, Brama Hedali, at the head of eighty Pandi or iron-smiths with their families, deserted their country. They were pursued as far as the river Pamali in Brebes, but effected their escape, and were received with open arms at Majapahit; Chiong Wandra, on demanding that the Pandi should be delivered up, received a positive refusal, and in consequence declared war against his half brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.

title.en: Batara Kala: The Devourer of Children and the Ruwatan of the Dalang
title.zh: 卡拉神：食子之神與達朗的淨儀

region.en: Wayang purwa cycle, Central and East Java
region.zh: 哇揚戲班，中爪哇與東爪哇

texts.period: Javanese wayang purwa tradition (the Murwakala cycle); documented in the wayang repertoire

source.archive: Javanese wayang tradition (documented in the wayang lakon repertoire)
source.work: The Murwakala legend of Batara Kala (wayang purwa)

summary.en: The wayang's great explanation of child-death: Batara Kala, the ogre of time, devours children — the deaths of the young are his appetite walking through the village. The dalang performs the play Murwakala as a ruwatan, a cleansing: the puppet rite stands between Kala and the household, teaches the ogre his limits, and sends the family out from the performance washed of the debt his hunger represents.
summary.zh: 哇揚戲對夭折之解釋：卡拉神——時間之巨魔——吞噬孩童；幼兒之死即其食慾巡行於村。達朗（戲偶師）以哇揚戲《穆爾瓦卡拉》行『魯瓦坦』淨儀：偶戲立於卡拉與家宅之間，教知巨魔其限，使全家自戲場洗淨其飢餓所代表之債。

sensitivity.note: Living wayang ritual theology; paraphrase respectfully.

texts.canonical_translation: Based on the wayang purwa tradition of the Murwakala play; paraphrase only

narrative.en:
The Batara Kala cycle is the wayang's charter of mourning: it explains why children die and what the community can do about it.

BEGINNING: THE OGRE OF TIME. In the wayang theology Batara Kala is the devourer set over the span of things — the great ogre whose hunger is time itself. Children are his proper prey; the death of a child in the village is his passing, and the fear of him hangs over every cradle.

MIDDLE: THE PLAY AS BARGAIN. The dalang answers with the play Murwakala, performed as a ruwatan — a cleansing rite — for households under threat: the story of Kala's origin and his restraint. In the play's theology Kala was created in the beginning as a force of consumption, and the gods themselves had to negotiate the terms of his eating: the boundaries within which he may take, and the signs by which a child is spared.

END: THE CLEANSING OF THE HOUSE. The performance is the medicine: the family that watches the play from beginning to end — the dalang's voice speaking the ogre's part, the shadows falling on the screen — stands inside the pact, and the child at risk is presented to the story and passed through it. The ruwatan closes with the community's eating together; the debt the ogre represents has been paid in spectacle.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle (1) explains child-mortality theologically without blaming the parents; (2) gives the dalang his highest office — exorcist, not entertainer; (3) charters the wayang performance as a protective rite (the play performed for endangered children); and (4) supplies the origin-of-death cluster with the Javanese devourer-of-children form. The ruwatan's choreography gives the theology its practice: households sponsor the play for children whose births or circumstances mark them, the dalang recites the ogre's origin and his negotiated limits, and the family sits inside the story's shelter from the first shadow to the last. The wayang's protective office explains the dalang's social standing: he is not an entertainer who happens to chant sacred tales but a ritual technician whose night-work stands between Kala and the cradle. The theology's compassion is its distinctive note: the child's death is laid to the ogre's appetite rather than to the parents' fault, and the community's answer is spectacle rather than accusation — the debt represented by hunger is paid in a story told to its face. In the wayang repertoire the Murwakala stands beside the Mahabharata plays as one of the few lakon performed for necessity rather than occasion.
narrative.zh: 卡拉神故事乃哇揚戲之喪慟憲章：解釋孩童何以夭折、社群能做何事。開篇：哇揚神學中，卡拉神是掌管時限之吞噬者——其飢餓即時間本身；孩童乃其應得之獵物，村中幼兒之死即是他的路過，其名高懸於每一搖籃之上。中段：達朗以《穆爾瓦卡拉》一劇行魯瓦坦淨儀，為受威脅之家宅演出——講述卡拉之起源與其節制：劇中神學謂卡拉於太初受造為吞噬之力，諸神被迫與之談判其食之條界——他可取之界、以及孩童得免之徵。結尾：演出即是藥：全家自首至尾觀戲——達朗之聲代巨魔發言、影落幕上——即立於盟約之內；受險之孩童被呈於故事之前、並穿越之。魯瓦坦以社區共食作結；巨魔所代表之債已以演劇償付。功能：不咎父母而神學地解釋夭折、賦達朗以最高職分（驅邪者而非娛樂者）、以哇揚演出為護佑之儀（為危孩而演）、並為『死亡之由來』母題群供給爪哇式『食子者』形態。

functions: Explains child-mortality theologically without blaming the parents
Assigns the dalang his highest office: exorcist of the devourer
Charters the wayang performance itself as a protective rite for endangered children
Javanese form of the origin-of-death cluster: the devourer of children

variants.name: Murwakala play variants
variants.summary: Village and court tellings differ in Kala's parentage and in the terms of his restraint.

title.en: Nyi Roro Kidul: The Queen of the Southern Sea

region.en: Pelabuhan Ratu and the south coast of Java

texts.period: Javanese court tradition (documented from the Mataram court period); earlier South-Sea motifs recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: The legend of the Queen of the Southern Sea (Javanese court tradition); cf. Raffles 1817, the South Sea at Kandang West

summary.en: The green-clad spirit-queen of Java's south coast: Nyi Roro Kidul rules the Indian Ocean from the southern sea, is consort and guardian to the kings of Mataram and their successors, and takes to her green waters those she favours and those who offend. Green is her colour and not to be worn on her shore; the kings keep her chamber in their palaces; the harbour where her legend concentrates is named Pelabuhan Ratu — 'the harbour of the queen.'
summary.zh: 爪哇南海岸之綠衣靈后：洛羅·兀魯統轄南印度洋，為馬打藍諸王及其後嗣之后與守護者；受其寵者與犯其忌者皆被收於碧波之中。綠為其色，臨其岸不可著綠衣；歷代君王於宮中設其專室；其傳說所聚之港名『女王港』（Pelabuhan Ratu）。

sensitivity.note: Living court devotion and popular belief; paraphrase respectfully; note the earlier South-Sea casting legend recorded by Raffles as a motif-root.

passages.text: Nyi Roro Kidul, the queen of the southern sea, rules the ocean along Java's south coast; she is consort and guardian to the kings of Mataram and their successors, and the green sea-belt takes those she favours as it takes those who offend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese court legend of the Queen of the Southern Sea; not verbatim.

passages.text: Green is her colour and is not worn on her shore; the palaces of the kraton keep a chamber for her visits, and the harbour of her legend is named Pelabuhan Ratu — the harbour of the queen. The south coast's casting legends recorded in the older chronicles — the king thrown into the South Sea at Kandang West — are the motif's roots.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Javanese court legend, with the Raffles (1817) South-Sea motif noted; not verbatim.

title.en: The Princess of Gunung Ledang: A Phial of the Raja's Blood
title.zh: 利芒山公主：一瓶國王之血

region.en: Gunung Ledang (Mount Ophir), Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 利芒山（歐菲爾山，《馬來紀年》地理）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XXVII (the embassy to the Princess Gunung Ledang), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Sultan Mahmud of Malacca, widowed, sends Tun Mamed up the musical mountain to ask for the Princess Gunung Ledang. The way up runs through groves of spontaneously melodious bamboo and a garden where flowers recite pantuns, to a hall of bone roofed with hair; the princess, in the guise of an old woman, sets her price: stairs of gold and of silver from Malacca to the mountain, a gnat's heart and a moth's heart each seven platters broad, a vat of human tears, a vat of young betel-nut juice, a phial of the raja's blood — and one of the young prince's. The king consents to all but the blood.
summary.zh: 滿剌加蘇丹馬末喪偶後，遣敦·馬末登『樂音之山』向利芒山公主求婚。登山之途經自鳴之竹林與花樹吟班頓詩之園，至骨為牆、髮為頂之大殿；公主化為老嫗索價：自滿剌加至山之金梯銀梯、闊七盤之蚊心與蛾心、人淚一缸、嫩檳榔汁一缸、國王之血一瓶——及幼王子之血一瓶。王允一切，惟血不可。

sensitivity.note: The Annals' most famous supernatural-wooing episode; the blood-price is the moral hinge.

passages.text: The king said, 'I want to ask the Princess Gunung Ledang'; and Tun Mamed, sent first to clear the way, ascends a mountain of violent gusts and unsupportable cold, where the bamboos are spontaneously melodious, the forest deer are enchanted by their melody, and a garden of wonderful beauty holds flowers that recite pantuns and fruits that laugh and smile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: At a hall whose materials are of bone and its roof of hair, the princess — in the guise of an old woman, hunch-backed and bent threefold — delivers her answer: if the raja of Malaca wishes for her, he must first make a flight of stairs of gold, and another of silver, from Malaca to Gunung Ledang; and present a gnat's heart seven platters broad, a moth's heart seven platters broad, a vat of human tears, a vat of the juice of the young betel nut, one phial of the raja's blood, and one phial of the Prince Raja Ahmed's blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The whole is related to Sultan Mahmud Shah, who says that all these requests may be complied with, but that the taking of blood is an unpleasant business, and he has no inclination for it at all — the bride-price declined at the exact point where it asked for the life of his son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XXVII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Maro Cycle: The Dema Theology of Western Seram
title.zh: 瑪羅循環：西塞蘭之德瑪神學

texts.period: Recorded 1937-38 by the Frobenius Institute expedition (Ad. E. Jensen); published Jensen, Hainuwele, 1939, and Myth and Cult, 1963

source.work: The dema corpus of the Wemale of western Seram, incl. the Maro dance cycle (recorded with named informants)

texts.license: Jensen 1939/1963 quoted only as summary (copyright); dema narratives are community heritage — paraphrase only

summary.en: Around Hainuwele, the Frobenius expedition recorded the Wemale dema cycle: the primordial world of the dema-beings, the origin of the nine-night maro dance and its exchange, and the theology that all culture — dance, planting, death — rises from the acts and deaths of the dema. The corpus frames Hainuwele's murder as one episode in a complete moral history: killing is the price of sustenance, and the maro dance re-enacts it.
summary.zh: 弗羅貝尼烏斯探險隊於海努韋萊之外又錄得西塞蘭瓦馬勒人之德瑪故事群：原初德瑪存在之世界、九夜『瑪羅』舞與交換之起源、以及『一切文化——舞、耕、死亡——皆自德瑪之行與死而生』的神學。該故事群將海努韋萊之死納入完整道德史：殺戮為取食之代價，瑪羅舞即其重演。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era collection (1937-39), flagged; Seram communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only.

narrative.en:
The dema theology of western Seram, as reconstructed from the Jensen expedition's recordings, is Maluku's most systematic myth-cycle — the frame within which the Hainuwele story stands.

BEGINNING: THE WORLD OF THE DEMA. Before the present order, the world is inhabited by the dema — beings of the primordial time, neither gods nor animals, who act and die in ways that fix what the world will be. Their acts are the templates of things: each dema-death or dema-deed founds a species of plant, an instrument, a custom.

MIDDLE: THE MARO DANCE AND THE EXCHANGE. The great institution of the dema-time is the maro — the nine-night festival of dance and gift-exchange recorded with the Hainuwele story, in which the circle of dancers closes around the giver at the centre. The cycle tells how the maro was founded in the dema era and how its exchange binds clans to clans; the girl whose death defines the festival is buried at the dance-ground, and her body becomes the food plants — so that the festival's gifts are, in the theology, pieces of her, redistributed.

END: THE FALL INTO THE PRESENT. With the dema-era deaths, the world hardens into its present form: men are separated from the dema, death becomes the human condition, and the rituals — the maro, the funeral, the planting — are what remain of the passage. Jensen's famous reading is that the corpus encodes a theology of the origin of culture in primordial murder: killing is the price of sustenance, and ritual re-enacts it; the anthropological debate about his 'dema' category continues, but the corpus itself is Seram's, not the theory's.

FUNCTIONS. The cycle (1) grounds the maro festival as charter; (2) explains agriculture, exchange and death in one system; (3) supplies the dismembered-culture cluster with its eastern-Indonesian food-and-dance form; and (4) documents — through the named informants of the expedition notebooks — a complete regional theology before its twentieth-century transformations. The corpus's regional depth repays notice: the Frobenius expedition of 1937-38 recorded the Wemale narratives with named informants in its notebooks, and the published corpus in Jensen's Hainuwele (1939) and the later Myth and Cult arranged them into the dema-theology that became a benchmark of the history-of-religions school — a framework that later scholarship has both used and contested. What belongs to Seram itself is the narrative system: a primordial population whose deaths fix the world, a festival whose gifts are pieces of a buried girl, and an origin of culture in which killing is not an accident but the founding transaction. The maro's nine nights give the theology its calendar, and the funeral its doctrine: burial is planting, and the dead are the seed of the next crop. In comparative view the cycle stands with Hainuwele at the junction of the dismembered-creator myths (Purusha, Ymir, Pangu) and the exchange-festival charters of Melanesia and eastern Indonesia — producing, unlike the cosmic versions, not a universe but a meal, and not by a god's hand but by a community's.
narrative.zh: 據詹森探險隊錄音重建之西塞蘭德瑪神學，乃馬魯古最系統之神話群——即海努韋萊故事所處之框架。開篇：現存秩序之前，世界由德瑪居住——原初時代之存在者，非神非獸，其行與死規定世界之所將是；每一德瑪之死或行皆奠定一種植物、一件器物、一項習俗之原型。中段：德瑪時代之偉大制度即瑪羅——與海努韋萊故事一併錄得之九夜歌舞交換節；舞圈環繞居中之贈者而合攏。故事群敘述瑪羅如何奠基於德瑪時代、其交換如何綁定氏族；定此節日之少女葬於舞場，其身化為食糧之植物——故節日之贈品在神學上即她的碎片之再分配。結尾：隨德瑪時代之死亡，世界凝為今形：人與德瑪分離，死亡成為人之境遇；瑪羅、葬禮、耕作等儀式即通道之所餘。詹森之著名解讀：故事群以原初謀殺編碼『文化起源』之神學——殺戮為取食之代價、儀式即其重演；其『德瑪』範疇之爭論持續，但故事群本身屬於塞蘭，而非理論。功能：以憲章立瑪羅節、於一系統內解釋農耕、交換與死亡、為『碎身文化』母題群供給東印尼之『食與舞』形態、並經探險隊筆記中有名之報告人記錄了二十世紀轉型之前完整之區域神學。

functions: Charters the nine-night maro festival of dance and exchange
Explains agriculture, exchange and death within one system
Eastern-Indonesian form of the dismembered-culture cluster: food and dance from a dema body
Documents a complete regional theology through named informants before its modern transformations

variants.name: Hainuwele (the central dema myth)
variants.summary: The coconut-girl whose dismembered body becomes the clans' food plants — the corpus's central episode.

variants.name: Jensen's dema-theory debate
variants.summary: The 'dema' category as Jensen's interpretive frame; the corpus is Seram's heritage independent of the theory.

primary_sources.citation: Recorded 1937-38 by the Frobenius Institute expedition (Ad. E. Jensen) among the Wemale of western Seram; informants named in the expedition notebooks; published in Jensen, Hainuwele, Frankfurt 1939 (copyright), and Myth and Cult among Primitive Peoples, 1963.

secondary_sources.work: Adolf E. Jensen, Myth and Cult among Primitive Peoples
secondary_sources.citation: Jensen 1963, Chicago: University of Chicago Press — the dema-theology framework.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Colonial-era expedition materials; Seram and Maluku communities hold the heritage — paraphrase only, no verbatim ritual text.

passages.text: Before the present order the world is inhabited by the dema — beings of the primordial time whose acts and deaths fix what the world will be: each dema-death founds a species of plant, an instrument, a custom. The maro — the nine-night festival of dance and gift-exchange — is founded in the dema era; the girl whose death defines the festival is buried at the dance-ground and her body becomes the food plants, so that the festival's gifts are, in the theology, pieces of her redistributed among the clans.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Wemale dema corpus as summarized in the Jensen expedition materials; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of the Wemale dema corpus; not verbatim.

title.en: The Spectre Huntsman of the Malay Hills

region.en: Selangor hills, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪山丘（斯凱特採錄）

texts.period: Recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V, the Spectre Huntsman

summary.en: The Spectre Huntsman rides the forest trails at night with hound and spear — the leader of the spectral chase of the Malay hills, whose weapons are named in the charm-books: the lance singkabuana ('lion of the world'), the kris salngkisa. He is blamed for deaths in the forest, and his passing is read in the baying of unseen dogs.
summary.zh: 魅影獵手夜騎於林間小徑，帶獵犬與長矛——馬來山丘幽冥獵隊之主；符咒書中記其武器之名：長矛『辛卡布瓦納』（世界之獅）、克利斯『薩恩基薩』。林中暴斃皆歸咎於他；其過處，以無形獵犬之吠聲可辨。

passages.text: The Spectre Huntsman rides the forest trails of the Malay hills at night with hound and spear, leader of the spectral chase; the charm-books name his weapons — the lance singkabuana, 'lion of the world,' and the kris salngkisa. Deaths in the forest are laid to his passage, and his approach is known by the baying of unseen dogs — the Malay wild huntsman in the Skeat collection's fullest figure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V; not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.

title.en: Men Who Are Tigers: The Malay Were-Beast Lore
title.zh: 化虎之人：馬來獸化傳說

region.en: Malay Peninsula and Sumatra (shared lore, collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島與蘇門答臘（共享傳說，斯凱特採錄）

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the tiger and were-beast beliefs of the Malays

summary.en: In Malay belief certain men are tigers: the village tiger that passes by night may be a neighbour in his beast-shape, whose human clothes are found folded where the animal slept; such were-tigers do not eat their kin, spare their friends' herds, and can be recalled to human shape by recognition — a beast whose beastliness is a temporary and negotiable condition.
summary.zh: 馬來信仰中，某些人即是虎：夜行過村之虎可能是鄰人化身，其衣摺疊於獸睡之處；如此『化虎者』不食親屬、饒過友人之牛群，且可因相認而復人形——獸性在此是暫時可談判的狀態。

sensitivity.note: Were-beast folklore recorded 1900; careful not to frame any living community practice.

passages.text: In Malay belief certain men are tigers: the tiger that passes the village by night may be a neighbour in his beast-shape, his human clothes found folded where the animal slept. The were-tiger does not eat his kin and spares his friends' herds, and can be recalled to human shape by recognition — the beastliness a temporary and negotiable condition in the Skeat collection's tiger lore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.
